walkthroughs.body_html:
In Natural Theology (1802), William Paley imagines stumbling on a watch in a heath. Its intricate parts, arranged for a purpose, force the inference to a designer; a similar inference applies to the natural world.

Paley devotes long chapters to the eye, the hand, and bird migration, all instances of contrivance that point beyond chance.

Hume's Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), published posthumously, anticipated Paley. Philo argues that the world resembles an organism more than a machine, that we have observed only one universe, and that imperfections suggest a finite or apprentice designer.

The analogy, in short, is too weak to bear the weight of classical theism.

Richard Swinburne's The Existence of God (1979) revives natural theology as a cumulative Bayesian case. The regularity of nature, the existence of conscious beings, and the fine-tuning of physical constants all raise the probability of theism.

Swinburne argues that simple theism is a more elegant explanation than a multiverse hypothesis.
